lesson.title: Opioids: Borrowing the Body's Own Painkillers
lesson.summary: Opioids are agonists at mu opioid receptors, the same receptors the brain's own endorphins use to relieve pain, which explains both their power as painkillers and their overdose risk.
lesson.body:
Opioids are a class of drugs that includes natural compounds extracted from the opium poppy, such as morphine and codeine, semi synthetic derivatives like heroin and oxycodone, and fully synthetic versions like fentanyl. What unites all of them pharmacologically is that they are agonists at opioid receptors, especially the mu opioid receptor, the same receptor type that the brain's own endorphins and enkephalins normally activate to relieve pain and regulate mood.

This connection to the body's natural chemistry explains why opioids are such effective painkillers. Endorphins are released during injury, intense exercise, or stress to blunt pain signals traveling up the spinal cord and to produce a mild sense of well being. Opioid drugs simply activate that same system more strongly and for longer than the body's own endorphins typically do, which is why they remain a mainstay of pain treatment for injuries and surgery despite their serious risks.

The euphoria and reward that make opioids prone to misuse involve a second, indirect step. Mu opioid receptors sit on inhibitory GABA neurons within the ventral tegmental area, a small midbrain region that is a major source of the brain's dopamine reward pathway. Normally those GABA neurons keep nearby dopamine neurons in check. When an opioid activates the mu receptors on them, it suppresses those GABA neurons, releasing the brake on the dopamine neurons and letting them fire more freely, which increases dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens, a region central to feelings of reward and reinforcement.

Mu opioid receptors are not confined to the brain. They are also dense in the gastrointestinal tract, where their activation slows movement through the gut. This is why constipation is such a common and persistent side effect of opioid use, one of the few effects that does not fade much even after tolerance develops to the pain relieving and euphoric effects, since the gut's receptors adapt more slowly than the brain's do.

The same receptor activation that relieves pain also explains the deadliest risk of opioids. Mu opioid receptors are present in brainstem regions that regulate breathing, and strong activation there suppresses the automatic drive to breathe. Most fatal opioid overdoses come from this respiratory depression rather than from any direct toxic effect on the heart or other organs, which is exactly why the antagonist naloxone, described in an earlier chapter, is such an effective emergency reversal: by displacing the opioid from mu receptors without activating them, it restores normal breathing.

Because opioids act so directly and so strongly on a receptor system the brain relies on for its own pain and mood regulation, repeated use reliably produces both tolerance and, if use stops abruptly, withdrawal, two processes covered in detail in the chapters that follow.
